{{Short description|Extinct language spoken in Vanuatu}}{{More citations needed|date=January 2026}}{{Infobox language | name = Sowa | states = [[Vanuatu]] | region = [[Pentecost Island]] | extinct = c. 2000, with the death of Maurice Tabi | familycolor = Austronesian | fam2 = [[Malayo-Polynesian languages|Malayo-Polynesian]] | fam3 = [[Oceanic languages|Oceanic]] | fam4 = [[Southern Oceanic languages|Southern Oceanic]] | fam5 = [[North-Central Vanuatu languages|North-Central Vanuatu]] | fam6 = [[Central Vanuatu languages|Central Vanuatu]] | iso3 = sww | glotto = sowa1244 | glottorefname = Sowa | map = Lang Status 20-CR.svg | mapcaption = {{center|Sowa is classified as Critically Endangered by the [[UNESCO]] ''[[Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger]]''.}} }} '''Sowa''' was the original language of south-central [[Pentecost Island|Pentecost island]] in [[Vanuatu]]. In the 20th century it was totally displaced by [[Abma language|Apma]], a neighbouring language. Sowa was closely related to [[Ske language|Ske]], another south Pentecost language. Sowa was originally spoken on both western and eastern sides of Pentecost. The river at [[Melsisi]] formed the language's north-western boundary, and its range extended southwards to a creek near the village of Levizendam.{{Citation needed|date=January 2026}} Following the depopulation of Pentecost that occurred after the introduction of European diseases, men from Sowa-speaking areas were married women from other parts of Pentecost, who were mostly Apma speakers. As a result, by the 1960s, Apma had totally replaced Sowa as the predominant local language. The last native Sowa speakers died around the year 2000.{{Citation needed|date=January 2026}} Today, a few local people whose fathers or mothers were Sowa speakers still remember parts of the language, although none speak it fluently. A few local people compiled short written notes on Sowa in an attempt to ensure that the language was not lost. The only linguist to have studied Sowa while the language was still alive was David Walsh, who collected a vocabulary list in 1969.{{Citation needed|date=January 2026}} Chief Isaiah Tabi of [[Vanuu|Waterfall village]] and Andrew Gray, a British schoolteacher at [[Ranwadi High School|Ranwadi College]], have worked with speakers' children to try to reconstruct the basics of the language.{{cite book |last=Tabi Vahka |first=Isaiah |title=Tamzon Nan Dutmekan Lon Dolod Ne Sowa |year=2006 |trans-title=First Book of Our Language which is Sowa}}{{Cite book |last=Grey |first=Andrew |title=The Languages of Pentecost Island |publisher=Manples (BFOV) |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-9560985-4-2}} Some people in the former Sowa area see the language as a part of their cultural heritage and lament its loss. There is talk of reviving Sowa, although records are insufficient to allow a fully authentic restoration of the language.{{Citation needed|date=January 2026}} ==Status as a language== Sowa was closely related to neighbouring [[Ske language]]. In his 1976 survey of ''New Hebrides Languages'', [[Darrell Tryon]] classified Sowa as a separate language,{{cite book |last=Tryon |first=Darrell |author-link=Darrell Tryon |title=New Hebrides Languages: An Internal Classification |publisher=Pacific Linguistics |year=1976 |doi=10.15144/PL-C50 |doi-access=free}} calculating its cognacy with Ske at 77% (with 80% being the approximate threshold below which two forms are considered separate languages rather than mere dialects). However, in their 2001 survey, Lynch & Crowley did not recognise Sowa as a language, noting that Tryon's data suffered from significant margins of error.{{Cite book |last=Lynch |first=John |title=Languages of Vanuatu: A New Survey and Bibliography |last2=Crowley |first2=Terry |date=2001 |publisher=Pacific Linguistics |doi=10.15144/PL-517 |doi-access=free}} Using an updated word list, Andrew Gray calculated the cognacy of Sowa and Ske at 82%. Sowa's status as a language is therefore borderline if considered on the basis of cognacy figures alone. However, local people perceive Sowa very much as a distinct language and not as a Ske dialect, and there are significant grammatical and phonological differences between Sowa and Ske.{{Citation needed|date=January 2026}} ==Phonology== The [[consonants]] of Sowa were '''b''', '''d''', '''g''', '''k''', '''l''', '''m''', '''n''', '''ng''' (as in English "singer"), '''p''', '''r''', '''s''', '''t''', bilabial '''v''', '''w''', '''z''', and labiovelar '''bw''', '''mw''' and '''pw'''. Sowa appears to have lacked ''h'', although this letter occasionally appears in records of Sowa as a result of un-phonetic spelling and interference from other languages. There were fewer restrictions on the distribution of consonants than in [[Apma language|Apma]] and [[Raga language|Raga]]. However, it appears that consonants occurring at the end of an utterance were modified according to Apma-like rules, with ''b'', ''v'' and ''w'' converted to ''p'', ''d'' devoiced to ''t'', ''g'' devoiced to ''k'', and ''r'' dropped to produce a long vowel. Clusters of consonants within syllables were not permitted. Unlike in neighbouring [[Ske language|Ske]], there was no [[Prenasalized consonant|prenasalization of consonants]] in Sowa. In addition to the five standard [[vowels]] ('''a''', '''e''', '''i''', '''o''' and '''u'''), Sowa appears to have had mid-high vowels '''é''' (intermediate between ''e'' and ''i'') and '''ó''' (intermediate between ''o'' and ''u''), like in [[Ske language|Ske]] and [[Saa language|Sa]] languages. Long vowels ('''aa''', '''ee''', etc.) occurred as a result of the dropping of ''r'' at the ends of words, and are shown to have been distinct from short vowels by [[minimal pairs]] such as {{lang|sww|me}} "to be red" and {{lang|sww|mee}} (< {{lang|sww|mer}}) "to be black". ==Grammar== Because no linguist ever worked directly with a native Sowa speaker, the language's grammar is poorly known. However, some of the basics can be deduced from the phrases that are remembered.{{Citation needed|date=January 2026}} ===Pronouns=== Personal pronouns were distinguished by [[Grammatical person|person]] and [[Grammatical number|number]]. They were not distinguished by [[Grammatical gender|gender]]. Like in [[Ske language|Ske]], there was no distinction between [[Dual (grammatical number)|dual]] and [[plural]] in independent pronouns, but separate dual forms of subject markers did exist (see below).{{Citation needed|date=January 2026}} The basic pronouns in Sowa were: {| class="wikitable" |- ! colspan="2" | ! singular ! plural |- ! rowspan="2" | 1st person ! exclusive | rowspan="2" | nou | kamwam |- ! inclusive | éd |- ! colspan="2" | 2nd person | ék | kimi |- ! colspan="2" | 3rd person | ni | néé |} ===Nouns=== Nouns in Sowa were generally not preceded by [[Article (grammar)|articles]]. [[Plural]]ity was indicated by placing the pronoun {{lang|sww|néé}} ("them") or a number after the noun. Nouns could be either '''free''', or '''directly possessed'''. Directly possessed nouns were suffixed to indicate whom an item belonged to. For example: :{{lang|sww|dolo'''k'''}} = my voice :{{lang|sww|dolo'''m'''}} = your voice :{{lang|sww|dolo'''n'''}} = his/her voice :{{lang|sww|dolo'''n''' dasék}} = my mother's voice Possession could also be indicated by the use of '''possessive classifiers''', separate words that occur before or after the noun and take possessive suffixes. These classifiers were similar to those of [[Apma language|Apma]]: *''no-'' for general possessions (''nok wokat'', "my basket") *''bile-'' for things that are cared for, such as crops and livestock (''biled bó'', "our pig") *''a-'' for things to be eaten (''an bwet'', "his taro") *''me-'' for things to be drunk (''mem ré'', "your water") There was also an '''associative construction''', like that of [[Apma language|Apma]] and [[Ske language|Ske]], for possessions over which the possessor has no control (''vénu naik'', "my home island") The possessive suffixes were as follows: {| class="wikitable" |- ! colspan="2" | ! singular ! plural |- ! rowspan="2" | 1st person ! inclusive | rowspan="2" | -(i)k | -d |- ! exclusive | -mwam |- ! colspan="2" | 2nd person | -m | -mi |- ! colspan="2" | 3rd person | -n | (lengthened vowel) |- ! colspan="2" | Generic | colspan="2" | -gze |} A verb could be transformed into a noun by the addition of a '''nominalising suffix''' ''-an'': :{{lang|sww|bwal}} = to fight (verb) :{{lang|sww|bwalan}} = a fight (noun) [[Grammatical modifier|Modifiers]] generally came after a noun: :{{lang|sww|vat}} = stone :{{lang|sww|vat alok}} = big stone :{{lang|sww|vat iru}} = two stones Like in Apma, [[Demonstrative|demonstratives]] came in three main forms: :{{lang|sww|ga'''né'''}} = this one (near speaker) :{{lang|sww|ga'''no'''}} = that one (near listener) :{{lang|sww|ga'''zai'''}} = that one (away from both speaker and listener) === Verbs === Verbs were preceded by markers providing information on the subject and the [[Grammatical tense|tense]], [[Grammatical aspect|aspect]] and [[Grammatical mood|mood]] of an action. Like in Ske, these may have been complicated and subject to some variation, but the following commonly occur: {| class="wikitable" ! Person || Subject marker -
imperfective (present tense) || Subject marker -
perfective (past tense) || Subject marker -
irrealis (future tense) || English |-- | 1st person singular || {{lang|sww|mwi}} || {{lang|sww|ni, i}} || {{lang|sww|mwidi}} || "I" |-- | 2nd person singular || {{lang|sww|kimwa}} || {{lang|sww|ki, ti}} || {{lang|sww|kidi}} || "you" (singular) |-- | 3rd person singular || {{lang|sww|mwa}}, {{lang|sww|mwe}}, {{lang|sww|mo}}, {{lang|sww|mu}} || {{lang|sww|a}} || {{lang|sww|de}} || "he" / "she" / "it" |-- | 1st person plural (inclusive)|| colspan="3" | {{lang|sww|tapa, tapan, tapat}} || "we" (you and I) |-- | 1st person plural (exclusive)|| colspan="3" | {{lang|sww|kapa, kapan, kapat}} || "we" (others and I) |-- | 2nd person plural|| colspan="3" | {{lang|sww|kipa, pin, kipat}} || "you" (plural) |-- | 3rd person plural|| {{lang|sww|pa, pan, pat}} || {{lang|sww|ava, an, avat}} || {{lang|sww|deva, den, devat}} || "they" |} [[Plural]] subject markers all took at least three forms: one ending with -''n'', one ending with -''t'', and one ending with a vowel. The -''n'' forms appear to have been used where the following word began with a [[labial consonant]] such as ''b'', ''m'' or ''v'' ({{lang|sww|pan ba}} "they go"), the -''t'' forms where the following word began with a [[coronal consonant]] such as ''d'' or ''r'' ({{lang|sww|pat du}} "they stay"), and the vowel-ending forms with 'bound' verbs where the verb root began with a consonant cluster ({{lang|sww|palse}} "they see"). In first and second person plural forms, tense/aspect/mood may have been distinguished only through context and through accompanying words such as {{lang|sww|avé}} "it was..." and {{lang|sww|devé}} "it will be...". There is evidence for additional subject markers or verb-modifying particles used for [[Prospective aspect|prospective]], [[hortative]] and/or [[Hypothetical mood|hypothetical]] actions ({{lang|sww|tete va}} "let's go!") but these are poorly remembered. [[Dual (grammatical number)|Dual]] (two-person) forms incorporating a particle {{lang|sww|ra}} also existed, as in [[Ske language|Ske]], but are not well remembered. Like in Ske, there was an [[echo subject]] marker (singular {{lang|sww|la}}, plural {{lang|sww|lapa}}): :{{lang|sww|an ba '''lapa''' los}} = They went to swim [[Consonant mutation|Verb-initial consonant mutation]] occurred in a few common verbs such as {{lang|sww|ba~va}} "go", but does not appear to have been as widespread as in Apma and Ske: :{{lang|sww|mwa '''b'''a}} = it goes :{{lang|sww|a '''v'''a}} = it went [[Negation (linguistics)|Negative]] phrases began with {{lang|sww|atna}} ("absent"): :{{lang|sww|ni iko}} = I did it :{{lang|sww|atna ni iko}} = I didn't do it In the [[Imperative mood|imperative]], verbs could occur on their own (unlike in [[Apma language|Apma]] and [[Ske language|Ske]], in which they are always preceded by a subject marker). Verbs beginning with a pair of consonants acquired an extra vowel in this situation: :{{lang|sww|mwi lse}} = I see :{{lang|sww|Lese!}} = Look! [[Transitive verb|Transitive]] and [[Intransitive verb|intransitive]] verb forms were distinguished, like in [[Apma language|Apma]] and [[Ske language|Ske]]. Transitive forms were commonly followed with the suffix or [[Instrumental case|instrumental]] preposition {{lang|sww|né}}: :{{lang|sww|mwi rós}} = I move :{{lang|sww|mwi rós né vat}} = I move the stone Like neighbouring languages, Sowa made extensive use of [[stative verb]]s for descriptive purposes. Verbs in Sowa could be linked together in [[serial verb construction]]s. ==Sample phrases== {| class="wikitable" !
